$description: Instruments, their nested provisions, and cross-instrument relationships. Instruments carry NO dates: every date is a timeline record referenced by ID through 'milestones'. Instruments carry NO supervisor field: competence is an edge in institutions.json.
$note: legislative_status is a scalar describing position in the legislative process. It is deliberately NOT sufficient on its own: for staggered instruments the milestones array is authoritative about what actually applies and when. Entry into force and application are never merged. Treaty articles are modelled as provisions of the 'tfeu' and 'teu' instruments (tfeu:art-114, teu:art-4-2), so a legal basis is always a provision ID and never a special case.

instruments.full_name: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data

dna.objective: Protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data, and free movement of such data within the Union.
dna.risk_logic: Risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons.
dna.enforcement_mechanism: National supervisory authorities with the one-stop-shop for cross-border cases; EDPB consistency and dispute resolution.

sanction_ceiling.note: Two-tier: 2%/EUR 10m for the lower tier, 4%/EUR 20m for the upper tier. The figure recorded is the upper tier.

provisions.heading: Territorial scope
provisions.summary: Applies to processing by a controller or processor established in the Union, and to processing of data subjects in the Union by a controller not established in the Union where it relates to offering goods or services to them or monitoring their behaviour.
provisions.verification_note: Article number and heading recorded from general knowledge of the instrument; confirm the wording against the consolidated text before display.

provisions.heading: Principles relating to processing of personal data
provisions.summary: Six processing principles plus accountability: lawfulness, fairness and transparency; purpose limitation; data minimisation; accuracy; storage limitation; integrity and confidentiality.

provisions.heading: Lawfulness of processing
provisions.summary: Exhaustive list of lawful bases: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, legitimate interests.

provisions.heading: Processing of special categories of personal data
provisions.summary: Prohibits processing of special categories absent a narrow derogation.

provisions.heading: Automated individual decision-making, including profiling
provisions.summary: Protection against decisions based solely on automated processing producing legal or similarly significant effects. In force since 2018, and therefore the pre-existing European law of automated decision-making.

provisions.heading: Data protection by design and by default
Notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority
provisions.summary: 72-hour notification decision.

provisions.heading: Data protection impact assessment
provisions.summary: The conceptual ancestor of the DSA's Art. 34 systemic risk assessment and the AI Act's Art. 27 fundamental rights impact assessment.

provisions.heading: Designation of the data protection officer
provisions.summary: Mandatory where processing is carried out by a public authority or body, and in the other cases the Article specifies.
provisions.verification_note: Article number and heading recorded from general knowledge; confirm against the consolidated text.

provisions.heading: Supervisory authority
provisions.summary: Each Member State provides for one or more independent supervisory authorities.

provisions.heading: Competence of the lead supervisory authority
provisions.summary: The one-stop-shop: the authority of the controller's main establishment leads cross-border cases.

provisions.heading: Cooperation between the lead authority and other concerned authorities
General conditions for imposing administrative fines
provisions.summary: Two-tier penalty ceilings.

instruments.full_name: Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 on a Single Market For Digital Services

dna.objective: A single market for digital services, replacing the liability core of the 2000 e-Commerce Directive with a graduated due-diligence regime.
dna.risk_logic: Systemic risk (Art. 34), assessed by the provider and mitigated proportionately.
dna.enforcement_mechanism: Commission for VLOPs and VLOSEs; national Digital Services Coordinators for all lower tiers.

provisions.heading: Notice and action mechanisms
provisions.summary: Electronic notice mechanisms for sufficiently precise and adequately substantiated notices. Art. 16(3) provides that a compliant notice gives rise to actual knowledge or awareness for the Art. 6 liability exemption where it allows a diligent provider to identify the illegality without a detailed legal examination.

provisions.heading: Online interface design and organisation
provisions.summary: Ban on dark patterns. Art. 25(2) excludes practices covered by the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive.

provisions.heading: Online protection of minors
provisions.summary: Measures to ensure a high level of privacy, safety and security for minors, including a prohibition on advertising based on profiling where the recipient is known to be a minor.
provisions.verification_note: Article number and heading recorded from general knowledge; confirm against the consolidated text.

provisions.heading: Traceability of traders
provisions.summary: Online platforms allowing consumers to conclude distance contracts with traders must obtain and check specified trader information before allowing use of the service.
provisions.verification_note: Article number and heading recorded from general knowledge; confirm against the consolidated text.

provisions.heading: Very large online platforms and very large online search engines
provisions.summary: Designation threshold of 45 million average monthly active recipients in the Union.

provisions.heading: Risk assessment
provisions.summary: VLOPs and VLOSEs must diligently identify, analyse and assess systemic risks stemming from the design or functioning of their service, at least annually and before deploying functionalities likely to have a critical impact.

provisions.heading: Mitigation of risks
provisions.summary: Proportionate, effective mitigation, with the choice of measures left to the provider.

provisions.heading: Recommender systems
provisions.summary: At least one recommender option not based on profiling.

provisions.heading: Additional online advertising transparency
provisions.summary: Enhanced advertisement repository.

provisions.heading: Data access and scrutiny
provisions.summary: Art. 40(12) access to publicly available data; Art. 40(4) access to non-public data for vetted researchers, requested through the Digital Services Coordinator of establishment. Both purpose-limited to research on systemic risks.

provisions.heading: Competent authorities and Digital Services Coordinators
Competences
provisions.summary: Allocates supervision between the Commission (VLOPs and VLOSEs) and national Digital Services Coordinators.

provisions.heading: Fines
provisions.summary: Up to 6% of global annual turnover.

instruments.full_name: Regulation (EU) 2022/1925 on contestable and fair markets in the digital sector

dna.objective: Contestable and fair markets in the digital sector, through ex ante obligations rather than ex post proof of anticompetitive effect.
dna.risk_logic: Contestability and fairness. Designation is a binary switch, not a graduated tier.
dna.enforcement_mechanism: Exclusive Commission enforcement. No national enforcement route.

provisions.heading: Definitions
provisions.summary: The core platform service categories: intermediation, search, social networking, video sharing, communications, operating systems, browsers, virtual assistants, cloud, advertising.

provisions.heading: Designation of gatekeepers
provisions.summary: Quantitative presumption: substantial EU turnover or market capitalisation, at least 45 million monthly active end users and 10,000 yearly active business users in the Union, sustained over three financial years.

provisions.heading: Obligations for gatekeepers
provisions.summary: Self-executing prohibitions. 5(2) no combining personal data across core platform services without consent, with a genuinely equivalent less-personalised alternative. 5(4) no anti-steering. 5(6) no preventing business users raising non-compliance. 5(7) no requiring use of the gatekeeper's identification, payment or browser engine.

provisions.heading: Obligations susceptible of further specification
provisions.summary: 6(4) third-party app stores and sideloading. 6(5) no self-preferencing in ranking. 6(7) free and effective interoperability. 6(9) data portability. 6(10) business-user access to performance data.

provisions.heading: Obligation for gatekeepers on interoperability of number-independent interpersonal communications services
Fines
provisions.summary: Up to 10% of global annual turnover; 20% on repeated infringement.

provisions.heading: Cooperation and coordination with national competent authorities
provisions.summary: The Commission is the sole enforcer; national authorities support rather than enforce.

provisions.heading: Review
provisions.summary: Required a review by 3 May 2026.

instruments.full_name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence
instruments.status_note: In force since 2024. Prohibitions, AI-literacy, GPAI duties and governance apply; the high-risk tier does not yet. The scalar alone is insufficient — read the milestones.

dna.objective: Harmonised rules on artificial intelligence, structured as product-safety legislation: conformity assessment, technical documentation, notified bodies, CE marking, post-market monitoring.
dna.risk_logic: Four-tier risk pyramid — unacceptable, high, transparency, minimal — with a separate compute-based presumption for general-purpose models.
dna.enforcement_mechanism: AI Office for general-purpose AI models; national competent authorities for AI systems; conformity assessment and market surveillance.

provisions.heading: Definition of a general-purpose AI model
provisions.summary: Trained on broad data, displaying significant generality, capable of competently performing a wide range of distinct tasks and integrable into downstream systems, with an indicative floor around 10^23 training FLOP.

provisions.heading: Prohibited AI practices
provisions.summary: Manipulative or deceptive techniques; exploitation of vulnerabilities; social scoring; individual criminal-risk prediction based solely on profiling; untargeted facial-image scraping; emotion inference in workplaces and education; biometric categorisation inferring sensitive attributes; real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement, subject to narrow exceptions. Binds public authorities as well as firms.

provisions.heading: Classification rules for high-risk AI systems
provisions.summary: Two entry routes: 6(1) safety component of a product covered by Annex I harmonisation legislation; 6(2) falling within Annex III. 6(3) provides a filter where no significant risk of harm is posed, subject to documentation and registration.

provisions.heading: Responsibilities along the AI value chain
provisions.summary: A distributor, importer or deployer becomes a provider — assuming the full obligation set — if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk system, substantially modifies it, or modifies its intended purpose.

provisions.heading: Transparency obligations
provisions.summary: Users must be informed they are interacting with an AI system; synthetic content must be marked in a machine-readable format; deep fakes and AI-generated text on matters of public interest must be disclosed.

provisions.heading: Classification of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk
provisions.summary: 51(1)(a) high-impact capabilities or 51(1)(b) Commission decision. 51(2) supplies the operative presumption: cumulative training compute greater than 10^25 FLOP.

provisions.heading: Obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models
provisions.summary: Annex XI technical documentation; Annex XII information pack for downstream providers; a copyright compliance policy; a sufficiently detailed public summary of training content. 53(2) partially exempts genuinely free and open-source models, but not systemic-risk models.

provisions.heading: Obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk
provisions.summary: Model evaluation against standardised protocols including documented adversarial testing; assessment and mitigation of Union-level systemic risks; tracking and prompt reporting of serious incidents; adequate cybersecurity protection.

provisions.heading: Penalties
provisions.summary: Up to 7% of global annual turnover or EUR 35 million.

instruments.full_name: Regulation (EU) 2023/2854 on harmonised rules on fair access to and use of data
instruments.status_note: General application since September 2025; the Art. 3(1) design obligation, the switching-charge ban and the extension of unfair-terms rules to pre-existing contracts arrive later.

dna.objective: Fair access to and use of data — predominantly non-personal, industrial and machine-generated — reallocating control over it by default.
dna.enforcement_mechanism: National competent authorities; penalty levels set by Member States.

sanction_ceiling.note: Set by Member States rather than by the Regulation.

provisions.heading: Obligation to make connected product data accessible to the user
provisions.summary: Connected products must be designed and manufactured so that product and related service data are, by default, easily, securely and directly accessible to the user.

provisions.heading: Contractual terms concerning switching
provisions.summary: Mandatory contractual content for switching: maximum two-month notice period; 30 calendar day transitional period (or a justified alternative not exceeding seven months where technically unfeasible); at least 30 days data retrieval afterwards; full erasure once retrieval ends.

provisions.heading: Cybersecurity risk-management measures

instruments.full_name: Treaty on European Union

provisions.heading: National identity and essential State functions
provisions.summary: Reserves national security to the sole responsibility of each Member State. The structural source of the asymmetry between constraint on corporate and on state power.

relationships.summary: GDPR Art. 22 has governed solely-automated decision-making since 2018, including systems the AI Act classifies as minimal risk. The AI Act arrived into a field the GDPR already occupied.

GDPR Art. 35 DPIAs, DSA Art. 34 systemic risk assessment and AI Act Art. 27 fundamental rights impact assessment are three overlapping assessment duties that regulators themselves acknowledge are duplicated.

Content moderation is processing; ad repositories publish targeting data; Art. 40 access almost always entails personal data. The DSA tells platforms to be transparent while the GDPR tells them to minimise. EDPB guidance mediates the conflict but does not dissolve it.

Both regulate large platforms but on different axes: the DSA on systemic risk and due diligence, the DMA on contestability and fairness. Designation under one does not imply designation under the other.
The DMA operates alongside Articles 101 and 102 TFEU, not instead of them. Google received a separate EUR 2.95 billion Article 102 fine in September 2025.
DMA Art. 5(2)'s consent architecture is functionally a data protection provision enforced by a competition regulator.

The AI Act is product-safety legislation; the revised Product Liability Directive brings software and AI within strict product liability. The proposed AI Liability Directive, which would have covered the fault-based route, was abandoned.
Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 amends the AI Act, deferring the high-risk tier while leaving prohibitions, GPAI duties and transparency close to the original schedule.

PROPOSED amendment only. The Digital Omnibus proposes changes to the personal-data definition, a new Art. 41a, relocation of cookie consent to Art. 88a and a new Art. 88c. None is law; the proposal is stalled in Council.
Companion directives sharing a transposition deadline: NIS2 on cyber resilience, CER on the physical and organisational resilience of critical entities.
DORA is the sector-specific ICT resilience regime for financial entities, sitting against NIS2's horizontal baseline.
relationships.verification_note: The lex specialis characterisation is stated by the brief's framing rather than established from a primary source in this build.

relationships.summary: The CRA regulates the security of products with digital elements; NIS2 regulates the security of the entities that operate them.

The Data Act mandates open interoperability and the elimination of lock-in; the sovereignty requirements of the proposed Cloud and AI Development Act push toward highly secure, localised environments. The two pull in opposite directions.
The DSA replaced the liability core of the 2000 e-Commerce Directive with a graduated due-diligence regime.
Almost the entire digital rulebook rests on the internal-market harmonisation competence rather than on a speech, safety or morality competence. That choice shapes each instrument's form.

Article 4(2) TEU reserves national security to the Member States, and the AI Act does not apply to AI systems used for military, defence or national security purposes. This is the structural source of the asymmetry between constraint on corporate and on state power.
